prime.problem: Quicksort's speed depends on pivot luck and it scrambles equal keys. Sometimes you need a sort whose cost is the same on every input and which keeps ties in order: sorting records by several keys, sorting a linked list, or sorting a file bigger than memory.
prime.fits: Fourth sort. Quicksort put its work before the recursion; merge sort puts it after, in the merge. The merge is reused on the next card to count inversions, and divide and conquer later derives its n log n from the recurrence.
expect: stability: ties take the left run
prime.goal: Trace a bottom-up merge sort, derive why it's Θ(n log n) on every input, and explain what one character in the merge does to stability.

attend: Why can two sorted runs be merged in one pass, looking only at their front items?
Why is the number of passes ⌈log₂ n⌉ regardless of the input's order?
In the last merge of a, why is 82 copied without a compare?
What exactly changes between right < left and right <= left, and which cards end up in a different order?
Why does merge sort suit linked lists and files, where quicksort doesn't?

must: Two sorted runs → the smaller front item is the smallest remaining overall → take it, advance → one linear pass merges them (at most sum − 1 compares)
Width doubles each pass → ⌈log₂ n⌉ passes, each touching all n elements → Θ(n log n) on every input (20 passes, 2 × 10⁷ copies for 10⁶) → no worst-case surprise, unlike quicksort

Take from the right only when strictly smaller → equal keys always leave from the left run, which holds the earlier ones → stable → you can sort by a secondary key, then a primary key, and keep the secondary order within ties
elevated: Merging reads and writes in straight lines → works on linked lists (relink, no buffer) and external files (sequential reads) → but on arrays it needs an n-element buffer, so in-memory introsort is faster (0.031 s vs 0.072 s)
reference: the source copying the buffer back each pass

compress.prompt: From memory, draw the bottom-up passes for a 7-element array as three rows of runs (widths 1 → 2 → 4 → 7), write the recurrence beside them, and add one line on the tie rule that makes it stable.
checklist: merge = repeatedly take the smaller front item; one pass, linear
runs of 1 are sorted; widths double each pass
⌈log₂ n⌉ passes × n per pass = Θ(n log n), independent of input order
strict < on the right item keeps ties in input order: stable
costs an n-element buffer; great for linked lists and external sorting

retrieve.q: Explain why merge sort's best, average and worst cases are all Θ(n log n), when quicksort's range from n log n to n².
answer: merge sort always splits at the midpoint (or doubles width), so depth is always ⌈log₂ n⌉
every level moves all n elements regardless of values
quicksort's split point depends on the pivot's value, so its depth can reach n

retrieve.q: Walk through the width-2 pass on [27, 38 | 3, 43 | 9, 82 | 10]: which runs merge, in what order do items come out, and how many compares does each merge take?
You're sorting a 50 GB log file on a machine with 8 GB of RAM. Why is merge sort's structure the right starting point, and what does it cost you?
answer: sort memory-sized chunks, write them out as sorted runs, then merge the runs with sequential reads
the merge only needs the front of each run in memory
cost: extra disk passes and an output buffer; random-access sorts like quicksort or heapsort would thrash the disk

compare.q: On 10⁶ random floats numpy's stable (merge-based) sort took 0.072 s against introsort's 0.031 s. What do you buy with the extra 0.041 s, and when is it worth it?
answer: stability (ties keep input order) and a guaranteed O(n log n) with no pivot risk
cost: an n-element buffer and extra copying at every level
worth it for multi-key record sorts, linked lists, external sorting; not for plain numbers in memory

compare.q: This card counts passes; the divide-and-conquer card uses the master theorem on 2T(n/2) + n. Show both arguments give n log n, and say which one generalises to Karatsuba.
answer: passes: log₂ n levels × n work each
master theorem: leaves n^(log₂ 2) = n equal f(n) = n → case 2 → Θ(n log n)
only the master theorem generalises: Karatsuba's 3T(n/2) + n has growing levels, so "n per level" no longer holds

predict.q: Merge sort on already-sorted [3, 9, 10, 27, 38, 43, 82]: more compares than on a's 14, fewer, or the same? And what about the number of passes?
predict.answer: Fewer compares: 11 (counted by the n log n card's compare harness). Sorted runs make every merge exhaust the left run first, so the right run is copied without compares. But the passes stay at 3: bottom-up merge sort can't skip a pass, which is exactly what Timsort fixes by detecting runs already in the input (n − 1 = 6 compares on sorted input).

apply.task: Sort [5, 2, 4, 6, 1, 3] bottom-up by hand. For each width write the array after the pass and the compares it took. Then sort the cards [A 2, B 1, C 2, D 1] with the tie rule flipped to <= and say which pairs swap.
apply.done: Passes: width 1 → [2, 5, 4, 6, 1, 3], width 2 → [2, 4, 5, 6, 1, 3], width 4 → [1, 2, 3, 4, 5, 6], with 3 compares each (9 total). With <= the output is D1 B1 C2 A2: both ties flipped.
apply.hint: In the width-1 pass, [1] + [3] takes 1 compare too.
